items.finding: What the appendix documents. Online Appendix A defines the treatment as whether, in each state and month, legal strips were available in a way capable of a meaningful policy shock. For most jurisdictions it uses the statute's effective date from the NPHL database. It records seven state decisions. Five are departures: Alabama (June 1, 2022), Minnesota (July 1, 2021) and New Mexico (May 18, 2022) are coded untreated through 2022; North Carolina (source date 2019) is coded from July 22, 2022; the District of Columbia (April 11, 2019) from August 2019. Virginia and West Virginia were reviewed and keep the source's dates. Every state it does not discuss keeps the source's date.

items.finding: What kind of evidence the coding rests on, and from when. Minnesota and New Mexico rest on the authors' own reading of the statutes; New Mexico's implementing rules took effect on November 29, 2022. The other three rest on reports. Alabama: a drug threat assessment from 2023; a pharmacist survey that Table A1 places in 2025, in which 25.2% of pharmacists believed strips were still illegal; and a 2021 law-review article co-written by McMichael, one of the paper's authors. North Carolina: an undated UNC School of Government summary that calls the 2019 statute narrow, and a pharmacist survey from March–May 2022 that found two pharmacies dispensing strips. The North Carolina date was set three years after enactment. District of Columbia: its 2017–2019 enactments, and a local organization's statement of August 2019. The appendix calls this second group of evidence 'contemporaneous', but the Alabama evidence comes from after the data end (December 2022). Table A1 says North Carolina's pharmacy access stayed limited 'until 2022', but the survey shows only that access was limited in spring 2022. None of this evidence measures strip distribution or use.
items.reason: Added a key finding listing the evidence and its dates, and a reporting issue on the 'contemporaneous' label and the North Carolina date. Also added a reporting issue (editors' note): by the appendix's own account, North Carolina's 2019 statute already protected people testing drugs they intend to use and harm-reduction organizations that distribute strips. The Introduction names free distribution by such organizations as one way people get strips (p. 241), yet the three-year delay rests mainly on pharmacy access. Recorded under funding.affiliations_note that the Alabama decision cites a co-author's law-review article.

items.finding: ROBINS-I, bias in classification of interventions: serious stands, and is no longer provisional. The overall judgment (serious) stands.
items.reason: The appendix confirms the concern rather than removing it. (1) The indicator rests on the authors' state-by-state judgment of a 'meaningful policy shock', and they write that reasonable researchers may judge differently. (2) For 5 of the 19 jurisdictions with a source date in the window, the coding departs from the source. Three states with laws in force are coded as comparisons, and two dates are moved later, so about one in six of the post-law state-months implied by the source's dates is recoded. (3) The original article presented the dates as the source's, and the reasons were published only in 2026, partly on evidence from after the study period, so the coding cannot be shown to have been fixed before the outcome data were seen (ROBINS-I signalling question 3.3: probably yes). (4) The same implementation test was not applied to the other 12 jurisdictions coded at the statute date. (5) No results with the source's dates are reported. (6) The six undated states and the coding of dates within a month are still unstated. I did not raise it to critical: ROBINS-I reserves critical for extreme misclassification, and here the departures are documented with reasons, affect a minority of jurisdictions, and the other dates follow the source's effective dates. No domain judgment changed (serious, moderate, serious, moderate, moderate, moderate, moderate; overall serious), so verification.status stays ai-checked. checked_by now ends '; supplement read by AI reader 150 (27 October 2026)', and checked_on is 2026-10-27. The appendix's own argument, that some laws made no real difference for months or years, was added to the risk-of-bias reasoning as a further reason why a fall from the first month of each law is hard to attribute to strips. In all, 33 changes are logged in verification.disagreements; python3 -I scripts/check_card.py passes. The corrected card is data/study-cards/_incoming/drug-checking/sc_bhai_2025.json; the merged card file was not edited.

for_senior_author: Classification of interventions (sc_bhai_2025): I keep serious, now no longer provisional, and the overall judgment stays serious. Someone who gives more weight to two facts could argue for critical: the recoding was not disclosed when the results were first published, and the Alabama reasons rest on evidence from after the study period. Critical would make the card's overall judgment critical. The claim's certainty would stay very low (already the floor), but what the card can be cited for would narrow further. This is a judgment for you.

The cheapest test of whether the 7% depends on the authors' coding is a re-analysis of the public death data with the NPHL dates (Alabama, Minnesota and New Mexico counted from 2021–2022, North Carolina from 2019, DC from April 2019). Nobody has reported one. The card now names it under what_would_settle_it. Whether the editors should ask the authors for it is your call.

Davis et al. (2022), which the appendix names as its source database, is on file (PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Davis_2022_DrugCheckingLawUS.pdf). It has a reference record but no card, and it was not read in this round (outside this brief). It might show whether the six undated map states (Alaska, Massachusetts, Michigan, New York, Vermont, Wyoming) were legal before 2018, and whether the 12 Table 1 dates the appendix does not discuss match the source.
The question left open by adjudicator 149 (whether the Black-resident estimates need a subgroup note or a 'critical' rating) is not affected by the appendix and is still open.
